title: The Best Persistence Incorporates Follow up With a Contribution
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note defines persistence as staying committed to a worthwhile objective through a steady cadence of follow-up. It notes that worthwhile requests are seldom granted the first time, so persistence often separates acceptance from rejection, yet done poorly it reads as pressure and is found obnoxious. The author argues that repeating the same message with more urgency, more calls or exclamation points shows impatience, not commitment. The alternative is to follow up with a contribution, so that each return gives the other person something and not just a reminder. The note lists possible contributions, including a piece of finished work, a resource, an introduction, an update or taking a problem off their plate. Four short examples show the idea, from a cost analysis for an approver to a draft memo for a stalled decision-maker. The conclusion is that persistence depends less on how often we follow up than on what we bring each time.
points: Persistence succeeds when it is a cadence of useful follow-ups and fails when it is the same request repeated with more force.
A reminder asks the other person for something, while a contribution gives them something and a fresh reason to engage.
Contributions can be small and concrete: a short cost analysis, a draft agenda, a relevant article or the memo the other person would otherwise have to write.
Each valuable follow-up turns persistence from something others tolerate into something they appreciate.
quotes: Done poorly, persistence becomes pressure that pushes people away and is often viewed as obnoxious. Done well, persistence builds trust and momentum and is interpreted as passion and commitment.
Sending the same message again with more urgency, calling more often, or adding exclamation points does not show commitment. It shows impatience.
A reminder asks the other person for something, while a contribution gives them something.

The possibilities are endless: doing a small piece of work and sharing it, addressing a concern directly, sending a resource, making an introduction, sharing a relevant update or insight, taking a problem off their plate, offering an idea for solving a problem, compiling data.
A manager trying to get some time with a busy executive might send a draft agenda that makes the meeting easy to accept.
In the end, persistence is less about how often we follow up and more about what we bring when we do.
When persistence comes with a contribution, every return becomes a step forward rather than a reminder of what is still undone.
